title: Plist File Modification
summary: Property list files, usually called plists, are the key-value configuration files that macOS and its applications read at runtime. They exist in XML or binary form and store structured metadata in name and value pairs. An adversary who can write to one can change how a program or the system behaves without touching the program itself. Typical abuses include adding a path to the Dock preferences so an application appears in the Dock, setting the LSUIElement key so an app runs without a visible window or Dock icon, and inserting an LSEnvironment dictionary so the dynamic linker loads an attacker supplied library when the app starts. Plists that describe launch agents and launch daemons are read at login or boot, which also makes them a persistence mechanism. The artefacts are on-disk files with clear modification times, and macOS caches preference data, so defenders use file integrity monitoring, the unified log, and endpoint security tooling to spot unexpected plist edits made by a shell or a script interpreter.

beginner.definition: A plist file is a settings file on a Mac. It stores options as simple name and value pairs. Changing those settings can change how an app starts, hide its window, or make it load extra code. Attackers edit plists to keep their activity quiet and to survive a restart.
beginner.whyItMatters: These files are trusted by the system, so changes are easy to miss. One edited key can hide a program window or make harmful code start every time you log in. The program file itself stays untouched, so a simple file scan may find nothing wrong. This is why Mac defenders watch settings files, not only applications.
howItWorks: The attacker first gains the ability to write files as a user or administrator on the Mac.
They open a plist the system reads, such as a login item or an app settings file.
They add or change a key, for example a setting that hides the app window.
They may add an environment variable so the program loads an extra library at startup.
The system reads the changed file at login, at boot, or when the app next starts.
The new behaviour takes effect, and the tampered program quietly runs the attacker's code.
beginner.example: Imagine a block of flats with a noticeboard by the front door. The board lists simple rules, such as which gate the cleaner uses and when the bins go out. Residents trust the board completely and nobody rechecks it. Now imagine someone swaps one card on the board. It now says the cleaner should enter by the side gate and leave it unlocked. The building itself has not changed. The locks are the same, the walls are the same, yet everyone follows the new instruction. A modified plist file is that swapped card. The Mac keeps following it until somebody looks closely at the board.
takeaways: On a Mac, settings files can be as dangerous as program files.
Watch for plist changes made by shells, scripts, or unexpected user accounts.
Check login items and launch entries after any suspected compromise.

objectives: Describe what a plist file is and where macOS keeps these settings.
Explain how editing a plist can hide a program or add persistence.
Identify the log and file sources that record plist changes.
Explain why an unchanged application binary can still behave maliciously.
Outline a check for suspicious login items and launch agents on a Mac.
